CHOICE OF THERAPY Ulcerative colitis. • ACTIVE DISEASE: • mild to moderate In mild to moderate distal disease topical mesalazine, preferably in combination with an oral aminosali- cylate (mesalazine, balsalazide, or olsalazine), is the treatment of choice.3,4 Selected patients may benefit from oral sulfasalazine. Patients intolerant of topical mesalazine may be given a topical corticosteroid in- stead, though they are less effective.39 Suppositories are suitable for proctitis but foam or liquid enemas are required for more proximal disease (proctocolitis).3 Patients who fail to improve on a combination of oral aminosalicylate with topical mesalazine or corticos- teroid may require an oral corticosteroid (e.g. pred- nisone or prednisolone 40 mg daily).3,4,6 In left-sided or more extensive ulcerative colitis the preferred therapy is an oral aminosalicylate;3,4,6 olsalazine is best avoided in patients with pancolitis as it may be more likely to produce diarrhoea than mesalazine or balsalazide.3 There is some evidence that the benefits of aminosalicylates are dose relat- ed,4,6 and some controversy exists as to the optimum induction dose: use of higher doses initially may pro- duce better responses,4,6 but there is an increased risk of toxicity. Topical therapy is unlikely to be of benefit alone, but may be added for the relief of rectal symp- toms.3,6 Patients who fail to respond to oral aminosalicylates should be given an oral corticosteroid (as above). The corticosteroid should be reduced gradually (tapered) over several weeks once response is achieved.3,4 Since long-term treatment with corticosteroids is undesirable, patients with chronic active disease who are at high risk of relapse when the corticosteroid is withdrawn (corticosteroid-dependent disease) should be treated with a thiopurine (azathioprine or mercap- topurine) as a corticosteroid sparing drug.3,4 Thiopu- rines may also be effective in inducing remission in some patients who do not respond to oral corticoster- oids, although their slow onset of action is problemat- ic.4 In patients with more extensive, moderate to se- vere disease, infliximab may be an option.6 • severe Patients who present with severe colitis or who fail to respond to maximal oral treatment should be admit- ted to hospital for treatment with intravenous corti- costeroids.3,4,6 Patients should be given appropriate supportive therapy (including nutritional support if the patient is malnourished, intravenous antibacterials for infection, and blood transfusion if markedly anae- mic).3,4 Those who fail to respond to intravenous cor- ticosteroids within a few days
